story.head: The Sharks give up shots, and the Flames take them
paras: The Flames already played in San Jose once this season and left with a 2-1 win on Nov 2. The Sharks have won two in a row, while the Flames (9-11-1) lost 6-1 to Anaheim on Sunday. This is a Pacific Division matchup, with the Flames sixth (tied for 23rd in the NHL) and the Sharks fourth (tied for 18th). The Pacific has been the weakest of the four divisions so far.
The Flames’ record (.452) is about what their chances are worth. The Sharks’ record (.478) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.390), largely thanks to their goaltending.

The Flames take a lot of low-quality shots (32nd) and take more penalties than they draw (31st). Calgary has scored 2.43 goals a game, the fourth fewest in the league. As for the Sharks, they do a lot of their shooting from distance (2nd lowest), are one of the league’s most physical teams (2nd) and ice the puck a lot (32nd). The Flames are likely to get plenty of pucks to the net against the Sharks. Beyond that, both teams like to play fast, especially the Flames (2nd), so expect an open game.

Joel Farabee (7 G / 10 A / 17 P in 21 GP) leads the Flames in scoring, and Matt Coronato (4 G / 11 A / 15 P in 21 GP) isn’t far behind. For the Sharks, Macklin Celebrini (9 G / 18 A / 27 P in 21 GP) leads the way in scoring, with nine points in his last five games.

Dustin Wolf (4-5-1 / .875 SV% in 10 GS) is expected to start for Calgary, and Yaroslav Askarov (6-8-1 / .890 SV% in 15 GS) for San Jose. Askarov has a .925 save percentage in five starts against the Flames, well above his usual .885. Don’t read much into it: a goalie’s record against one team rarely holds up.
At home, Ryan Warsofsky likes to send Goodrow, Ostapchuk and Gaudette out against opponents’ fourth lines, so watch for them against Strömgren, Castagna and Suniev.
